verdict: The money loop is conserved and most [Confirmed] rules are built, but the economy's long-run behaviour follows from a few traceable mismatches: the 25% trader margin (DEC-098) was never carried into the producers' numbers or decisions, prices and wages drift apart under inflation, retained group cash has no adequate outlet, and the population rule's clamp plus migration makes decline the default. The player can also buy any NPC facility at a fixed nominal price, which dominates other strategies, and several documents still describe superseded rules. All numbers below come from reading code and data plus arithmetic, or are quoted from 04_Roadmap; nothing was run.

skimmed: Assets/_Game/Agents/MadeToOrder.cs (lines 60-300; the plan calculation itself was not read)
not_read: Assets/_Game/Agents: MerchantTraits.cs, MerchantVehicles.cs, Cargo.cs, DevelopmentState.cs, PolicyState.cs, FinanceState.cs, Guidance.cs, Lod.cs, Merchants.cs
Assets/_Game/Tests/EditMode other than the GroupTests lines above

findings.title: Long-run population decline comes from the growth clamp plus migration: villages' surplus is capped while people move to the towns that shrink
findings.evidence: Change per node is base 0 + 4% x (met/wanted - 1), clamped to [-4%, +1.3%]: `Fx.Clamp(change, -_config.PopulationMaxDecline, _config.PopulationMaxGrowth)`. Upside saturates at 132.5% supply. Migration only moves people from villages to towns, never back.
findings.failure_scenario: Roadmap year 30: city 84%, village 147%. City change is -0.64%; the village would be +1.88% but is capped at +1.3%. With an assumed 80% urban share, -0.51% + 0.26% = -0.25%, against the measured -0.28%. Year 60: city 89%, village 155%, assumed 85% urban gives -0.18%, exactly the measured figure. Population therefore falls while weighted supply is about 97%, and break-even needs city supply of 92-94%. Each village's surplus above 132.5% is wasted, and migration keeps moving weight onto the negative term.
findings.fix: Decide what steady state means, then either raise the base growth or the cap so break-even sits at the intended city supply, or measure population per head at nation level so a village surplus can offset town shortfall through migration. Add a town-to-village return flow when towns go short.

findings.title: The documented necessity elasticity of 0.5 acts as about 0.97, so small price rises above anchor read as famine
findings.evidence: Each quintile's elasticity is 0.5 x sqrt(0.2/share): multipliers 3.16, 2.58, 2.00, 1.41, 0.50. These average 1.93 rather than 1, and demand is the plain average of the five curves, not income-weighted.
findings.failure_scenario: City price 15% above anchor, shelves full and cash enough: Met/Wanted = 85.5% (20%: 80.7%; 30%: 71.0%), which is population -0.58% a year from price alone. That is the size of the measured city shortfall of 84-89%. The luxury curve at 1.5 is only about 1.55 times steeper, not the 3 times the config implies.
findings.fix: Normalise the sensitivities to mean 1, or weight the average, and retune; or state 0.97 as the real value in SYS_MARKETS. Separately, measure need satisfaction against what households can get rather than the anchor-priced quantity.

findings.title: At anchor prices most processing recipes lose money after the 25% margin, so the supply chain cannot clear at the prices the population rule needs
findings.evidence: Producers buy at 100% of price and sell at 75%. Weekly margin at anchor for a level-1 facility, after upkeep and 2.5% output wage: mill -28, malthouse -22, spinnery -28, smithy -78, coppersmith -29, tailor -39, bakery -47; smelters only +61 and +11, brewery +25, porridge +24. Smithy gross margin is negative before any cost: 6 x 90 x 0.75 = 405 against 6 x 70 = 420. Primary producers meanwhile make +150 to +585 and wagonworks +684.
findings.failure_scenario: For bread at anchor the bakery needs flour at or below 14.4 (90% of anchor), and the mill then needs wheat at or below 8.2 (82%). A merchant takes 0.75 of the town price, less toll and 1 coin a unit, and a normal group asks a 10% margin, so it buys village wheat only at about 4.3, about 45% of anchor. Any higher and carrying stops. The chain runs only with raw goods deep in glut; otherwise town prices sit above anchor, which through L2-02 and L2-01 lowers population. Added margin hops compound: each hop needs a price gap of at least 33%.
findings.fix: Retune recipes against offer prices (raise processed anchors or lower input ratios), or apply the margin to fewer passages, for instance only on household sales. Add a test that every recipe in a chain has a non-negative margin at some consistent set of prices near anchor.

findings.title: Investment, working-cash and bid decisions value output at list price, so groups build and fund facilities that lose money after DEC-098
findings.evidence: `margin += line.Quantity * PriceOf(node, line.Good)` in UnitMargin; `if (outputs <= inputs) return 0` in WorkingCashGap; `if (inputCost >= outputValue ...) return` in BidForInputs. All use the full price, though the seller receives 75%. RunFacility has no profitability check at all: with inputs in stock and cash it buys and produces.
findings.failure_scenario: Bakery at anchor: the investor sees a gain of about 120 a week and pays 6,000 inside the 8-year limit, while the real margin is -47 a week. A smithy shows +56 and really makes -78. Bids push an input price up to the output's full list value, where every unit made loses up to 25%. Groups then top these facilities up from retained cash and bonds until the debt limit, and each bankruptcy is refinanced by the group or the nation's households.
findings.fix: Value output at TraderOffer in UnitMargin, WorkingCashGap, BidForInputs and AidsAreWorthIt, and have RunFacility skip a run whose inputs cost more than the output's offer value.

findings.title: Defense purchases remove stock twice but pay once
findings.evidence: `Stock[c] -= (int)units; Demand[c] = ...Demand[c] + units` with no matching Supply add. Every other purchase (MarketFlows.Buy, ProductionJob.UseInput, BuyLoad) passes the units through Supply into Demand, and the job has no Supply array. The kernel then computes `available = s + st; traded = min(d, available); remaining = available - traded`.
findings.failure_scenario: Stock 100, army buys 10: stock is 90, demand 10, and repricing leaves 80, so 20 units are gone for 10 paid. Purchases cover all stock by value, food included, every 4 weeks, at 6% of the nation's spendable reserve a year. The extra demand also lowers what households can be delivered (DeliveredValue, Deliverable), so necessities are taken from them without payment.
findings.fix: Add the units to Supply in DefensePurchaseJob, as MarketFlows.Buy does. This changes the golden hashes.

findings.title: Upkeep, output wages, facility values and buffers stay nominal while the price index multiplies, shifting income from wages to profit
findings.evidence: `_defUpkeep[d] = _db.Config.FacilityUpkeep[...]` is fixed at start, and the output wage uses GoodBasePrice, while anchors scale with PriceIndex. Default minting (3% of 20M metal value on a 5M supply) gives an index of about 2.05 at year 10, 3.4 at year 30 and 4.4 at year 60; the roadmap's 'about 33M coins' at year 60 over two continents is near 3.3 (minting policy lowers it).
findings.failure_scenario: A wheat farm at anchor pays 80 in wages out of 900 at index 1, and the same 80 out of 3,060 at index 3.4. Towns' necessities at anchor cost 3.4 times as much while wages per facility do not move, so city budgets depend ever more on transfers, and profit flows to dividends and on to L2-07. FacilityInvestment.Wanted compares price with unindexed base, not the 'anchor price' DEC-080 names: at index 3.4 a good at 30% of anchor passes. Payback also gets easier each year because project cost is nominal, and merchants' wage buffers lose real value.
findings.fix: Multiply upkeep, output wage base, facility value, start cash and merchant buffer by the continent's PriceIndex, or derive them from anchors, and compare with the anchor in Wanted.

findings.title: Interest groups retain 75% of dividends with no adequate outlet, so idle money accumulates there, against the [Confirmed] 80% payout
findings.evidence: groups.payout_permille is 250 (DEC-080), but SYS_INTEREST_GROUPS states [Confirmed] about 80% and DEC-061 says the same. Outflows are only: investment (at most 2 projects per node a year, and only with plan >= 80%, price >= base, stock short and inputs at hand), 5% a year lobbying, 0.5% a week into bonds above twice start cash where bonds are on sale, and top-ups.
findings.failure_scenario: The roadmap records groups holding 17.8M at year 60 and marks the cause unsettled, out of about 33M coins (a roadmap figure from an earlier measurement). Profits rise with L2-06 while households and towns stay short, so the state has to issue bonds and public wages for towns while over half the money sits with owners. Trials in the roadmap already show payout changes moving the result, so this is a live lever.
findings.fix: Pay out above a working-capital level per group, scaled with its facilities, at a share high enough to hold group cash stable, and record the new rule in place of the 80% text. Keep the investment share explicit.

findings.title: Any NPC facility can be bought remotely at a fixed nominal price, which breaks state monopolies and dominates every other use of money
findings.evidence: Validate checks only ownership, the price and coins of the facility's continent: no presence at the node, no seller's refusal and no state-owned check. Value is linear in level (`FacilityValue * Level`) while output is level x (1 + 0.25(level-1)). Player output skips the plan (`if (FacilityOwner[f] == OwnerIds.Player) return output`), and warehouse overflow sells itself against the whole float, outside the [Confirmed] half-float limit for producers.
findings.failure_scenario: A wheat farm or iron mine costs 3,000 plus its cash and earns about 580 a week at anchor, payback 5 weeks; with wheat at 40% of anchor it is still about 130 a week, payback about 23 weeks, against 2-7% a year from deposits and bonds. A level-5 secondary facility asks 40,000 for 10 times output and 5 times upkeep, while building those levels costs 80,000 on top of the first level's 8,000. The player can buy every iron mine in a nation, a state monopoly under DEC-055, and so hold the tools every primary producer needs. DEC-107 notes this question is open. The price does not rise with inflation (L2-06).
findings.fix: Price a facility on its earnings or output, indexed; let owners refuse, or exclude state-owned types unless privatized (P12c); require presence or an agent to buy; and apply the float limit to overflow sales.

findings.title: Villages' idle coins (the roadmap's untraced 15-18M) follow from what their markets carry: they can buy only food, raw goods and a few luxuries
findings.evidence: Village markets carry grain, ore, textile, provisions and exotic at Low and Mid only: no cloth, drink, tools or High and Best grades. Household wishes count only for cells that exist and can deliver, so the budget's share reaches 1 quickly and the rest stays as cash. Wages keep arriving: 50% of local upkeep, and PayNationWages also pays villages by weight, so part of the 'wages leaving for towns' under DEC-077 comes back.
findings.failure_scenario: A village's cheap food costs far less than its income, leftover cash has almost nothing to buy, and only 1% a week of cash beyond 26 weeks goes to traders' loans. Village 'supply' of 147% also measures only food, while a city's need includes clothes and ale, so the two figures are not comparable. This matches the roadmap's village hoard, though the amount was not measured here.
findings.fix: Let villages buy clothing and drink (at least Low and Mid), or send surplus cash to towns through rent or a higher wage-away share paying towns only; and report supply on one common basket.

findings.title: Core towns are worst supplied because they take their classes' people but get no extra producers or investment room
findings.evidence: `Population[core] += Population[n]` moves class people, and core demand also gets +5% a point. Producer slots exist only for village and city levels, so nation and region classes have none to hand over despite DEC-104's wording. Investment caps every node at the same 24 facilities.
findings.failure_scenario: Roadmap: ordinary town 1.18M people, 93% of necessities; region core 1.70M, 82%; capital 2.25M, 78%. A capital has about twice the people on the same 14 starting slots (plus core-only workshops moved in) and the same investment cap, with 10% higher demand per head. The roadmap lists this as 'why is not settled'.
findings.fix: Scale producer slots and investment.max_per_node with a core's population or strength, or give nation and region levels producer counts that the core inherits. Measure the result, since core-only workshops also change the picture.

findings.title: After DEC-104 companies own no merchant groups, because ownership tests a home level that absorption moved to city level
findings.evidence: Merchants spawn with `nodes.Absorbed ? nodes.Core[n] : n` as home, and owners are chosen by `nodes.LevelOf(node) <= WorldLevel.Region` on that home, which is now always false. AgentTable.Scale keeps the true level. The test computes `large` the same way, so it passes on the wrong result.
findings.failure_scenario: All nation- and region-scale groups go to the core town's private enterprise, against the [Confirmed] company 'with facilities and merchant groups across regions'. Toll-paying stake (PolicySystem: `h.InputValue += stake`) moves from companies to families, so companies' toll stance turns more protectionist, and a failed large group's start cash comes from a small family and then the households.
findings.fix: Use `agents.Scale[a] <= (byte)WorldLevel.Region` in AssignOwners and in the test, and record new golden hashes.

findings.title: NPC merchants' insurance premiums go to households, not guilds, against DEC-061, which starves the guild safety net
findings.evidence: `HouseholdCash[node] += premium;` and refunds come from the same households. The player's trip pays premiums to `MoneyLedger.InsuranceGuild`. DEC-061 says 'insurance premiums go to the guild', DEC-055 says guilds run the insurance, and SYS_BANKING names the origin city's guild.
findings.failure_scenario: Guilds fund association top-ups but never receive NPC premiums, their largest natural income; policies moved heavily after DEC-099 (512k a year in premiums per the roadmap, in coins that should have been guild income). The roadmap already saw guild cash falling from 65k to 26k and 'the safety net running down'. Refunds are also capped by the origin node's household cash rather than a guild's reserves.
findings.fix: Route premiums and refunds through InsuranceGuild as the player's trip does, after the job, using a per-node accumulator like TollsByNode.

findings.title: Seized cargo and contract deliveries are paid the full price, against the [Confirmed] rule that traders pay any seller the price less 25%
findings.evidence: SellCargo uses `int price = _markets.Price[cell]`; the merchant cargo seizure uses `_markets.Price[cell]`; Deliver charges the buyer's float `-units * sell` at the full price. Only the player's sale, the overflow sale, producers and merchants apply the margin.
findings.failure_scenario: A player holding a load worth 10,000 at list gets 7,500 by selling it, but 10,000 of debt relief by letting a loan go overdue and having the bank sell the cart or warehouse, so default pays 33% better on that cargo. Each contract delivery drains the destination float by a third more than a normal sale.
findings.fix: Use TraderOffer in both seizure paths and in contract delivery.

findings.title: The player's insurance refunds coins lost but its premium counts only cargo, so a nearly empty cart insures all carried coins for almost nothing
findings.evidence: `insurance = options.Insurance ? config.InsurancePremium.MulInt(valueHere) : 0` uses cargo value, yet `refund = Insurance ? config.InsuranceRefund.MulInt(value) : 0` also applies when `loss == EncounterLoss.Cash`, where value is 30% of the coins. The NPC path's comment says 'The policy covers no coins'.
findings.failure_scenario: A player with 100,000 coins and an empty cart buys insurance for premium 0. On a cash encounter they lose 30,000 and get 24,000 back, paid by a guild or the origin's households. Coin risk falls by 80% for free, and NPCs have no such cover, against DEC-015's same-rules intent.
findings.fix: Refund cargo losses only, as for NPCs, or base the premium on coins plus cargo.

findings.title: Paying for goods from a deposit ignores the bank-run withdrawal limit
findings.evidence: BankTransferCommand caps a run's withdrawals at 10% of the deposit, once a week. BuyGoodsCommand takes `bank.PlayerDeposit[nation] -= cost - fromCoins` with no check of FinancialEventKind.
findings.failure_scenario: During a run a player with a 50,000 deposit is limited to 5,000 a week in coins, but can buy 50,000 of goods at a branch the same week, as far as the bank holds the coins, and carry them off. The bank's coins leave faster than DEC-044 allows.
findings.fix: Apply the same cap and the one-a-week rule to deposit payments, sharing a helper with BankTransferCommand.

findings.title: Import bills are recorded only by aggregate flows, so with every node detailed the state's import score is always zero
findings.evidence: The only write is `Imports[payer] += quantity * pay` in MerchantFlowJob, which skips detailed nodes. DetailedMerchantJob never writes Imports, and lod.mode is 1 under the [Confirmed] DEC-100.
findings.failure_scenario: DEC-072 [Confirmed] says projects are chosen from 'what they spend on imports'. In play harbor and highway always score 100 and paving 120, whatever a nation imports, so paving always ranks ahead of them while unpaved routes remain.
findings.fix: Record imports in the detailed path when a group from another nation or continent sells; a sale at a node outside the group's home nation is the natural trigger.

findings.title: Glutted goods settle at about 12% of anchor and stock never decays, so overproduction is paid for and piles up indefinitely
findings.evidence: With pressure near -1 the step is clamped to -15% a week and the pull is +2% of the gap, so the fixed point is 0.02/0.17 = 11.8% of anchor; the roadmap measures village wheat at 11-15%. Plans stay at 10-100% of capacity, there is no spoilage, and SellToMarket pays for all output as far as the float can.
findings.failure_scenario: A market in glut still pays producers 9% of anchor for every unit and adds it to stock: the roadmap lists 2.2M wheat, 900k beans and 1.1M vegetables idle. Stock also enters effective supply at 25%, so a large pile holds the price at the floor for years after production adjusts, and each such unit has drained traders' coins with no buyer.
findings.fix: Add stock decay by good (food fastest), and either let traders stop buying beyond a number of weeks of demand or let plans reach zero for goods not made to order.

findings.title: Several [Confirmed] rules have no implementation, and the roadmap's P16 status is wrong
findings.evidence: No closure of a facility losing money for two years, and no group road paving (DEC-054, DEC-065); searches found neither. DEC-065's 'at most one project per group a year' is contradicted by 2 per node, with a single richest group able to take several nodes. P16 is marked 'Ready' though InvestmentSystem is built. Ranks and ruin (DEC-063) and managers (DEC-064) are unbuilt as the roadmap admits; SetFacilityControlCommand changes a flag production ignores. DEC-106's exception awaits the user's confirmation per DEC-107.
findings.failure_scenario: Without closures, a structurally loss-making facility (L2-03, L2-04) goes bankrupt and is refunded by its group or households again and again. A player can switch a facility to Automated and nothing changes. A ruined player has no game over. A reader of the roadmap would rebuild P16 from scratch.
findings.fix: Build closure first, since it is a real outflow of bad capacity. Mark P16 partly built and record the 2-per-node change as a decision against DEC-065. Ask the user to confirm the DEC-106 exception.

findings.title: Household spending is not split by quintile as the [Confirmed] DEC-061 rule says: one pot and one budget share serve all
findings.evidence: HouseholdCash.Cash is per node and NecessityBudgetFactor is a single share. Quintile shares appear only as elasticity multipliers, so the Pareto rule of DEC-049 ('top 20% move 80% of market money') has no monetary effect.
findings.failure_scenario: A town whose budget covers 70% of necessities cuts every income class alike, instead of the poorest going short while the top quintile still buys. The dividend rule's 'top quintile of the home node' cannot be honoured either, so luxury demand and hardship do not follow income distribution.
findings.fix: Either hold cash per quintile, or decide against it and change the [Confirmed] text, with budget factors derived from the shares.

findings.title: Design documents state superseded rules as current
findings.evidence: Branches in every city [Confirmed] vs only at seats (DEC-104). Nation markets supplied [Confirmed, DEC-068] vs classes hold no market. Budget 26 weeks vs 13. Growth 0.8% at full supply vs config base 0. Payout 80% vs 25%. Merchants without guards vs DEC-085/099. Index on coin supply vs published total. 'Every node has exactly one market', 9,250 merchants, a one-coin pull always vs DEC-091. Roadmap 'Balance' figures of nation 4%. 'Cities keep four smithies' [Confirmed, DEC-069] with no such spawn rule: AgentsModule draws at random, and DEC-104 moves smithies to cores. A class comment says merchants stay on their continent.
findings.failure_scenario: A later implementer following a [Confirmed] line, such as branches in every city or four smithies per city, would undo a newer decision, and neither older decision is marked as changed.
findings.fix: Add 'Changed by' links to DEC-032, DEC-068 and DEC-069, get the user's ruling where a [Draft] overrode a [Confirmed], and update the listed lines.

findings.title: 'Special goods' means two different things in [Confirmed] rules
findings.evidence: DEC-021 and SYS_LICENSES: 'Selling special goods requires a license', with iron_tools the only such good. DEC-096 and DEC-103 call spice, silk, fur and amber 'special goods', and those have requires_license 0.
findings.failure_scenario: Reading the two [Confirmed] lines together, spice sold without a license breaks a rule. The user's actual intent for continental goods and licensing cannot be told from the documents.
findings.fix: Rename one set, for instance 'continental goods', and record whether they need licenses.

findings.title: Bonds and traders' loans repay a share of what remains, so they are not paid off over their stated term
findings.evidence: `Math.Max(1, _bonds.Face[r] / weeks)` uses the current face, giving geometric decay. Interest `rate.MulInt(Face) / 52` truncates to zero for a holding below about 1,300 at 4%.
findings.failure_scenario: A state bond 'paid off over 20 years' still has 36.8% of its face owing after 1,040 weeks, a company bond likewise after 10 years, and a trader loan after 52 weeks. Debt limits therefore stay fuller and for longer than planned, and the many small household holdings can earn nothing.
findings.fix: Store the original instalment on the row, or accept decay and correct DEC-097 and DEC-092; carry interest remainders.

findings.title: The published money total leaves out noble purses, so the price index runs slightly low
findings.evidence: ContinentMoney counts `houses.Cash[node]`, but MoneyTotals.Recompute has no NobleState. It also drops negative balances, so the total can exceed real money when arrears exist. MoneyTotal is documented as 'every coin held, counted once'.
findings.failure_scenario: With houses holding part of the income tax (30% of a village's tax before aid), the published total is below the coin supply by the purses' size, on my estimate about 1%, and DEC-062's index and the exchange rate inherit that.
findings.fix: Add noble cash to MoneyTotals and add a test that the published total equals ContinentMoney when no balance is negative.

findings.title: Sales have no slippage within a turn and purchases from stock do not raise a price, so large loads trade at the posted price
findings.evidence: Buy adds q to supply and demand and removes q from stock, so wanted minus effective supply changes by only +0.25q and stays negative while stock remains. Sell is capped only by the float. DEC-006 rejected instant impact, so this is by design, but its size was not tested against ship capacity.
findings.failure_scenario: A player ship carrying 2,400 size of spice sells it all at one posted offer in a market holding 65-230 units abroad (roadmap figures), and the price falls at most 15% next week. Roadmap city prices of 44% at home and 143% abroad give about 16 a unit after freight, roughly 39,000 a trip against a 5,000 ship, as far as home stock and the foreign float allow. NPC buying likewise does not close a village-to-town gap until stock runs out.
findings.fix: Keep DEC-006 but limit a week's sale to a multiple of the cell's weekly demand, or ask the user whether a depth limit is acceptable.

findings.title: Supply contracts carry licensed goods without a license check
findings.evidence: WidestGap and Deliver never consult NeedsLicense or HoldsLicenses, while merchant sales do: `if (NeedsLicense(node, good) && !HoldsLicenses(a)) continue`.
findings.failure_scenario: An unlicensed merchant group signs a contract on iron tools and delivers them into a town's market each week, against the [Confirmed] 'the others cannot sell licensed goods'. Contract delivery also has no toll, which DEC-087 allows only as a [Draft] exception to [Confirmed] DEC-015.
findings.fix: Refuse the contract when a merchant seller or buyer lacks the license, or have the user confirm contracts as an exception.

strengths: Money conservation: I traced wages, fees, tolls, ship trades, exchange, lobbying, bond purchases and sales, bills, trader loans and new operators through MoneyLedger, Purses, Credit, BankCommands and TravelCommands, and found no path creating or destroying coins (protested bills are claims, not coins; noble purses are counted in the audit even though not in the published total).
Round-trip trading at one market cannot profit: buying at price and selling at 75% loses a quarter (TradeCommands.cs).
Withdrawing a facility's profit does not dodge income tax: the withdrawal limit holds back the tax so far, and capital moves shift the book's start (FacilityCommands.cs:35, IncomeTax.cs:77).

Loans against deposits are no money pump: one loan per bank, loan-to-value of 50%, 10% interest added up front against 2% on deposits, and early repayment keeps the interest (BankCommands.cs, BankSystem.cs).

Exchange round trips lose the 3% fee each way, and yearly rate steps between continents are too small to beat it from the mint arithmetic (BankCommands.cs:130, Currency.cs:203). This rests on arithmetic, not a measured run.
DEC-105 holds in the three builders I checked: state projects, subsidies and investors all test FacilityPlaces.IsLand (StateProjectSystem.cs:230, SubsidySystem.cs:147, FacilityInvestment.cs:161).

DEC-106 is built as stated, with only the DEC-107 exception: a group that neither sold nor left sets off (MerchantJob.cs:233, MerchantJob.cs:249). DEC-102 also holds: the player and their groups never take bills (MerchantJob.cs:481, ProductionJobs.cs:285).
The status-quo bias of DEC-060 and the minting opposition are built as written (PolicySystem.cs:483, PolicySystem.cs:546).
